pron_note: Not "in-SOO-lar" — the first syllable takes the weight.
means:
Literally **of an island**; almost always used figuratively: **closed off from outside influence, narrow in outlook, interested only in one's own circle.**

The charge isn't hostility — it's *unexposed*. An insular community hasn't rejected the wider world so much as never bothered to look at it, and has grown small-minded by default. That makes it the standard cool, analytical word for describing whole institutions and countries as much as people: an insular department, an insular village, an insular foreign policy. Compare **aloof**, which is personal chilliness by choice; insularity is a whole worldview shrunk to fit one small place.
trick_line: **Insular = INSULATED** — the same walls that keep the heat in keep new ideas out.
trick_unpack: Insulation isn't malice, it's just a barrier — which is exactly why insular people and places end up narrow without ever deciding to be.
sentences: Decades of unchallenged prestige had left the faculty **insular**, citing chiefly one another and reviewing chiefly themselves.
He grew up in such an **insular** little town that meeting someone from two counties over counted as travel.
etymology:
Latin **insula** = *"island."* The figurative sense is the literal one: island-shaped thinking, cut off by water.

The root pays out widely: **isolate** (put on an island), **peninsula** (*paene* "almost" + *insula* — almost an island), **insulate** (wall off), and **insulin** — named for the *islets* of Langerhans, little islands of cells in the pancreas.
one_line: Narrow-minded and cut off from outside influence.
